summary: Defines a framework for centralized conferencing, where participants on call signaling protocols such as SIP, H.323, or ISUP exchange media in a centralized unicast conference. It defines logical entities, naming, and the set of protocols that fit around them. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Many people on different phone systems can join one meeting hosted by a central server. This paper explains the parts and how they fit.

questions: what is a sidebar in conferencing
subtitle: The parts, names and data model for a conferencing system built around one central server, whatever signaling the callers use.

tldr.problem: Conference participants may use different call signaling protocols such as SIP, H.323 or ISUP, and richer features like scheduling, sidebars and floor control need a shared model so that products from different vendors can interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: The framework puts a central focus in a star around the participants, describes each conference as a conference object cloned from blueprints, names it with identifiers, and lists the complementary protocols for control, notification and floor control.
tldr.outcome: It is a framework rather than a wire protocol: the XML data model and the conference control protocol are left to separate documents, and SIP is the only signaling protocol a system is REQUIRED to support.

today: RFC 5239 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2008. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it stands as published.

sections.title: The Centralized Conferencing Model
sections.content:
A centralized conference is an association of endpoints, the conference participants, with a central endpoint, the focus. The focus keeps a separate call signaling interface with each participant, so the call signaling graph is always a star. The framework covers participants using SIP, H.323, Jabber, Q.931 or ISUP, and is compatible with the SIP Conferencing Framework in RFC 4353.

The system is built around a conference object, which represents the conference at each stage of its life. The logical elements are a conference control server, a floor control server, any number of foci, and a notification service. Each has a matching protocol: a conference control protocol (CCP), a floor control protocol such as the Binary Floor Control Protocol (BFCP), a call signaling protocol, and a notification protocol such as SIP Notify. A system may support only a subset of these.

Media can be centralized, with sessions between a media mixer controlled by the focus and each participant, or decentralized as a multicast or multi-unicast mesh. The concepts map clearly to the centralized media model, and the decentralized case is left for future study.
sections.eli5: Everyone talks to one host in the middle, like spokes on a bicycle wheel. The host passes things along, so the callers never need to talk to each other directly.

sections.title: Conference Objects and Policies
sections.content:
The conference object has the type conference information, which is extensible. It holds the description (times and duration), membership (roles, capacity, names), signaling, floor information, sidebars, and mixer algorithm, inputs and outputs. The same object type represents the system capabilities, a reservation of resources, and the state of an ongoing conference. The exact XML schema is defined in a separate document, referred to as XCON-COMMON.

A core subset can be represented using the conference type of the SIP conference event package in RFC 4575. The wider data model adds media mixing details and floor controls, so authorized clients can change the mixer behavior through the focus.

Conference policies are the rights, permissions and limitations for operations on an object. Rights are read or write access, typically by role. Detailed permissions and limits are outside the scope of this framework. A system should provide a default user role that only allows participation through the default signaling, and notifications must be filtered so that only authorized users receive specific data.
sections.eli5: Each meeting has a fact sheet listing who is invited, what kinds of sound and video it has, and who may change what. The same kind of sheet is used before, during and after the meeting.

sections.title: Identifiers for Conferences and Users
sections.content:
Three identifiers tie the system together. The conference identifier is a call signaling protocol-specific URI that names a conference focus and its conference instance. A conference object can have several, one per signaling protocol, and there is a one-to-one mapping between an active conference object and a focus. A conference factory is one way to generate them.

The conference object identifier is a unique URI the system MUST allocate for every blueprint, reservation and active conference. Once a conference exists, a user MUST use it to manipulate conference data or use advanced features. It maps to other identifiers such as the BFCP confid, and the mapping can be sensitive, so it is not generally given to ordinary participants.

The conference user identifier MUST be allocated to every user. It is REQUIRED in CCP requests so the system knows who issues a command and can apply policy. If a user joins through signaling such as SIP and has none, one MUST be assigned. A system is REQUIRED to support SIP as the default call signaling protocol; others such as ISUP are OPTIONAL.
sections.eli5: A conference has three kinds of name tags: one for the phone number you dial in on, one for the meeting's fact sheet, and one for each person, so the host knows who is asking for what.

sections.title: The Cloning Tree and Scheduling
sections.content:
Every conference object is created by cloning, either from a parent object or implicitly from a default system conference blueprint, a static object describing a typical conference the system supports. The metaphor is cloning rather than inheritance because it is object replication. When cloned, the link to the parent may be kept or dropped. If dropped, the child is independent and is not affected by the parent. If kept, the parent can mark data elements as parent enforceable, which the child cannot change on its own.

In an ad hoc conference, the server copies a blueprint into a new active conference, which becomes independent of the blueprint and gets a new conference object identifier, conference identifier and focus. In the advanced case, a client lists blueprints, clones one into a conference reservation, edits it within system ranges, and may ask the server to create child reservations. At the start time, an active conference is cloned from the reservation.

Scheduling uses the iCalendar object specification in RFC 2445. A CCP request carries a reservation and an iCal object; one iCal object can describe a recurring series. To change only a range of a series, the system clones a child reservation that is not independent, with its own conference object identifier.
sections.eli5: Starting a new meeting is like photocopying a template form. You can fill in your copy however you like, unless the template marked some lines as locked.

sections.title: Signaling, Notification and Floor Control
sections.content:
Participants ask to establish or join a conference using call signaling. After checking policy, the focus accepts, sends a progress indication (for instance for a parked call awaiting moderator approval), or rejects. Later CCP requests to add or delete participants are checked against policy and carried out through the focus.

The notification service sends updates about conference state to authorized parties. SIP-based notification uses RFC 3265 with conferencing specifics from RFC 4575, and the user identifier and role filter what each user sees. The conference control protocol itself is specified in separate documents.

Floor control is not mandatory. BFCP in RFC 4582 lets an authorized client grant, deny or revoke access to a floor. Messages must identify the conference by its conference object identifier, the user by its conference user identifier, and the floor. With SDP, these map to the confid, userid and floorid attributes.
sections.eli5: You knock on the host's door to get in. A board tells everyone who just arrived. If only one person may talk at a time, a chair hands out the turn.

sections.title: Scenarios: Sidebars, Whispers and Coaching
sections.content:
The framework tests its model against scenarios, shown at a high level and noted as illustrative only. A client can ask for blueprints, reserve a conference from one and then activate it. A moderator can add a party with a CCP request, or mute one, which marks the party as recvonly so their media is not mixed. Other participants may be told through notifications, depending on policy.

A sidebar is a separate conference instance that exists only inside a parent conference. It is a clone that is not independent, and it cannot outlive its parent or include members from outside it. An internal sidebar lets two people talk privately while keeping the main video. An external sidebar can include a new guest. A whisper is one-time media to specific participants, for example a ten minute warning announced only to the chair.

Sidebars also build other features. Floor control for an analyst briefing keeps analysts muted in the main conference and moves them to a sidebar to speak, with the moderator as floor chair. Observing and coaching lets a supervisor hear a call, or sit in a sidebar with an agent so only the agent hears the coaching.
sections.eli5: A sidebar is a whispering corner in the same room. A few people step into it to talk, and the room stays open.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists attacks such as an endpoint listening to a conference it is not authorized to join, disconnecting or muting other users, and theft of service by creating conferences it should not. Protocols that handle confidential information need confidentiality and integrity, and it is RECOMMENDED that all protocols that interface with the conferencing system implement TLS. To limit denial of service, it recommends requiring authentication and authorization of every client.

PINs are discussed carefully: some are as short as 3 digits, and over a fast interface thousands of guesses per second are possible, so PINs are not appropriate on interfaces with fast or many simultaneous queries. Identity privacy has three visibility levels: hidden, anonymous and public. Because every user gets a conference user identifier, signaling-specific identifiers need not be shared with other participants.
sections.eli5: Bad guests might sneak in or switch off other people's microphones. The host should check who each guest is and use secret codes that are hard to guess.
